Solution of the polynomial moment problem Thanks: The research of the first author was supported by the ISF grant no. 979/07

F. Pakovich, M. Muzychuk
Abstract.

In this paper we give a solution of the following “polynomial moment problem” which arose about ten years ago in connection with Poincaré’s center-focus problem: for a given polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) to describe polynomials q⁡(z)q(z) orthogonal to all powers of P⁡(z)P(z) on a segment [a,b][a,b].

Key words and phrases: 
Center-Focus problem, moments, Cauchy type integrals, S-rings
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 30E99; Secondary 34C99; 20C05; 12F10

1. Introduction

In this paper we solve the following “polynomial moment problem”: for given P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] and distinct a,b∈ℂa,b\in{\mathbb{C}} to describe q⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]q(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] such that

(1) ∫abPi​(z)​q​(z)​𝑑z=0\int^{b}_{a}P^{i}(z)q(z){\rm d}z=0

for all i≥0i\geq 0.

The polynomial moment problem was posed in the series of papers [2]-[5] in connection with the center problem for the Abel differential equation

(2) d​yd​z=p⁡(z)​y2+q⁡(z)​y3.\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}z}=p(z)y^{2}+q(z)y^{3}.

with polynomial coefficients p⁡(z),q⁡(z)p(z),q(z) in the complex domain. For given a,b∈ℂa,b\in{\mathbb{C}} the center problem for the Abel equation is to find necessary and sufficient conditions on p⁡(z),q⁡(z)p(z),q(z) which imply the equality y⁡(b)=y⁡(a)y(b)=y(a) for any solution y⁡(z)y(z) of (2) with y⁡(a)y(a) small enough. This problem is closely related to the classical Center-Focus problem of Poincaré and has been studied in many recent papers (see e.g. [1]-[9], [29]).

The center problem for the Abel equation is connected with the polynomial moment problem in several ways. For example, it was shown in [4] that for the parametric version

d​yd​z=p⁡(z)​y2+ε​q​(z)​y3\frac{{\rm d}y}{{\rm d}z}=p(z)y^{2}+\varepsilon q(z)y^{3}

of (2) the “infinitesimal” center conditions with respect to ε\varepsilon reduce to moment equations (1) with P⁡(z)=∫p⁡(z)​𝑑z.P(z)=\int p(z){\rm d}z. On the other hand, it was shown in [7] that “at infinity” (under an appropriate projectivization of the parameter space) the system of equations on the coefficients of q⁡(z)q(z), describing the center set of (2) for fixed p⁡(z)p(z), also reduces to (1). Many other results concerning connections between the center problem and the polynomial moment problem can be found in [7]. These results convince that a thorough description of solutions of system (1) is an important step in the understanding of the center problem for the Abel equation.

There exists a natural condition on P⁡(z)P(z) and Q⁡(z)=∫q⁡(z)​𝑑zQ(z)=\int q(z){\rm d}z which reduces equations (1), (2) to similar equations with respect to polynomials of smaller degrees. Namely, suppose that there exist polynomials P~​(z),\tilde{P}(z), Q~​(z),\tilde{Q}(z), W⁡(z)W(z) with deg​W​(z)>1{\rm deg\,}W(z)>1 such that

(3) P⁡(z)=P~​(W⁡(z)),Q⁡(z)=Q~​(W⁡(z)).P(z)=\tilde{P}(W(z)),\ \ \ \ \ \ Q(z)=\tilde{Q}(W(z)).

Then after the change of variable w=W⁡(z)w=W(z) equations (1) transform to the equations

(4) ∫W⁡(a)W⁡(b)P~i​(w)​Q~′​(w)​𝑑w=0,\int^{W(b)}_{W(a)}\tilde{P}^{i}(w)\tilde{Q}^{\prime}(w){\rm d}w=0,

while equation (2) transforms to the equation

(5) d​y~d​w=P~′​(w)​y~2+Q~′​(w)​y~3.\frac{{\rm d}\tilde{y}}{{\rm d}w}=\tilde{P}^{\prime}(w)\tilde{y}^{2}+\tilde{Q}^{\prime}(w)\tilde{y}^{3}.

Furthermore, if the polynomial W⁡(z)W(z) in (3) satisfies the equality

(6) W⁡(a)=W⁡(b),W(a)=W(b),

then the Cauchy theorem implies that the polynomial Q~′​(w)\tilde{Q}^{\prime}(w) is a solution of system (4) and hence the polynomial q​(z)=Q′​(z)q(z)=Q^{\prime}(z) is a solution of system (1). Similarly, since any solution y⁡(z)y(z) of equation (2) is the pull-back

(7) y​(z)=y~​(W​(z))y(z)=\tilde{y}(W(z))

of a solution y~​(w)\tilde{y}(w) of equation (5), if W⁡(z)W(z) satisfies (6) then equation (2) has a center. This justifies the following definition: a center for equation (2) or a solution of system (1) is called reducible if there exist polynomials P~​(z),\tilde{P}(z), Q~​(z),\tilde{Q}(z), W⁡(z)W(z) such that conditions (3), (6) hold. The main conjecture concerning the center problem for the Abel equation (“the composition conjecture for the Abel equation”), supported by the results obtained in the papers cited above, states that any center for the Abel equation is reducible (see [7] and the bibliography there).

By analogy with the composition conjecture it was suggested (“the composition conjecture for the polynomial moment problem”) that, under the additional assumption P⁡(a)=P⁡(b),P(a)=P(b), any solution of (1) is reducible. This conjecture was shown to be true in many cases. For instance, if a,ba,b are not critical points of P⁡(z)P(z) ([9]), if P⁡(z)P(z) is indecomposable ([19]), and in some other special cases (see e. g. [4], [23], [22], [25]). Nevertheless, in general the composition conjecture for the polynomial moment problem fails to be true. Namely, it was shown in [18] that if P⁡(z)P(z) has several “compositional right factors” W⁡(z)W(z) such that W⁡(a)=W⁡(b)W(a)=W(b), then it may happen that the sum of reducible solutions corresponding to these factors is a non-reducible solution.

It was conjectured in [20] that actually any non-reducible solution of (1) is a sum of reducible ones. Since compositional factors W⁡(z)W(z) of a polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) can be defined explicitly, such a description of non-reducible solutions of (1) would be very helpful, especially for applications to the Abel equation (cf. [7]). However, until now this conjecture was verified only in a single special case (see [21]).

Meanwhile, another necessary and sufficient condition for a polynomial q⁡(z)q(z) to be a solution of (1) was constructed in [23]. Namely, it was shown in [23] that there exists a finite system of equations

(8) ∑i=1nfs,i​Q​(Pi−1​(z))=0,fs,i∈ℤ, 1≤s≤k,\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{s,i}Q(P^{-1}_{i}(z))=0,\ \ \ \ \ \ f_{s,i}\in{\mathbb{Z}},\ \ \ \ \ \ 1\leq s\leq k,

where Q⁡(z)=∫q⁡(z)​𝑑zQ(z)=\int q(z){\rm d}z and Pi−1​(z),P^{-1}_{i}(z), 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, are branches of the algebraic function P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z), such that (1) holds if and only if (8) holds. Moreover, this system was constructed explicitly with the use of a special planar tree λP\lambda_{P} which represents the monodromy group GPG_{P} of the algebraic function P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in a combinatorial way. By construction, points a,ba,b are vertices of λP\lambda_{P} and system (8) reflects the combinatorics of the path connecting aa and bb on λP\lambda_{P}.

A finite system of equations (8) is more convenient for a study than initial infinite system of equations (1). In particular, in many cases the analysis of (8) permits to conclude that for given P⁡(z),a,bP(z),a,b any solution of (1) is reducible (see [23]). In this paper we develop necessary algebraic and analytic techniques which allow us to describe solutions of (8) in the general case and to prove that any solution of (1) is a sum of reducible ones. So, our main result is the following theorem.

Theorem 1.1.

A non-zero polynomial q⁡(z)q(z) is a solution of system (1) if and only if Q⁡(z)=∫q⁡(z)​𝑑zQ(z)=\int q(z){\rm d}z can be represented as a sum of polynomials Qj​(z)Q_{j}(z) such that

(9) P(z)=P~j(Wj(z)),Qj(z)=Q~j(Wj(z)),𝑎𝑛𝑑Wj(a)=Wj(b)P(z)=\tilde{P}_{j}(W_{j}(z)),\ \ \ Q_{j}(z)=\tilde{Q}_{j}(W_{j}(z)),\ \ \ {\it and}\ \ \ W_{j}(a)=W_{j}(b)

for some polynomials P~j​(z),Q~j​(z),Wj​(z)\tilde{P}_{j}(z),\tilde{Q}_{j}(z),W_{j}(z).

Note that since conditions of the theorem impose no restrictions on the values of P⁡(z)P(z) at the points a,ba,b the theorem implies in particular that non-zero solutions of (1) exist if and only if the equality P⁡(a)=P⁡(b)P(a)=P(b) holds. Indeed, if P⁡(a)=P⁡(b)P(a)=P(b) then for any Q~​(z)∈ℂ​[z]\tilde{Q}(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] the polynomial Q​(z)=Q~​(P​(z))Q(z)=\tilde{Q}(P(z)) is a solution of (1) since we can set W⁡(z)=P⁡(z)W(z)=P(z) in (3), (6). On the other hand, if Q⁡(z)Q(z) is a solution of (1) then equalities (9) imply that P⁡(a)=P⁡(b)P(a)=P(b).

The paper is organized as follows. In the second section we give a detailed account of definitions and previous results related to the polynomial moment problem. In particular, starting from system (8), we introduce a linear subspace MP,a,bM_{P,a,b} of ℚn\mathbb{Q}^{n} generated by the vectors

(fs,σ⁡(1),fs,σ⁡(2),…,fs,σ⁡(n)),σ∈GP, 1≤s≤k,(f_{s,\sigma(1)},f_{s,\sigma(2)},\,...\,,f_{s,\sigma(n)}),\ \ \ \sigma\in G_{P},\ \ \ 1\leq s\leq k,

and study its basic properties.

It follows from the definition that MP,a,bM_{P,a,b} is invariant with respect to the permutation matrix representation of the group GPG_{P}. In the third section of the paper, written entirely in the framework of the group theory, we describe a general structure of such subspaces. More generally, we describe subspaces of ℚn\mathbb{Q}^{n} invariant with respect to the permutation matrix representation of a permutation group GG of degree nn, containing a cycle of length nn. Roughly speaking, we show that the structure of invariant subspaces of ℚn\mathbb{Q}^{n} for such GG depends on imprimitivity systems of GG only. We believe that this result is new and interesting by itself.

Finally, in the fourth section, using the description of GPG_{P}-invariant subspaces of ℚn\mathbb{Q}^{n} and results and techniques of [23], we prove Theorem 1.1.

2. Preliminaries

In this section we collect basic definitions and results concerning the polynomial moment problem. In order to make the paper self-contained we outline proofs of main statements.

2.1. Criterion for H^​(t)≡0\hat{H}(t)\equiv 0

For P⁡(z),Q⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z),Q(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] and a path Γa,b⊂ℂ\Gamma_{a,b}\subset{\mathbb{C}} connecting different points a,ba,b of ℂ{\mathbb{C}} let H⁡(t)=H⁡(P,Q,Γa,b,t)H(t)=H(P,Q,\Gamma_{a,b},t) be a function defined on ℂ​ℙ1∖P⁡(Γa,b){\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus P(\Gamma_{a,b}) by the integral

(10) H⁡(t)=∫Γa,bQ⁡(z)​P′​(z)​d​zP⁡(z)−t.H(t)=\int_{\Gamma_{a,b}}\frac{Q(z)P^{\prime}(z)dz}{P(z)-t}.

Notice that although integral (10) depends on Γa,b\Gamma_{a,b} the Cauchy theorem implies that if Γ~a,b⊂ℂ\tilde{\Gamma}_{a,b}\subset{\mathbb{C}} is another path connecting aa and bb, then for all tt close enough to infinity the equality

H⁡(P,Q,Γ~a,b,t)=H⁡(P,Q,Γa,b,t)H(P,Q,\tilde{\Gamma}_{a,b},t)=H(P,Q,\Gamma_{a,b},t)

holds. Therefore, the Taylor expansion of H⁡(t)H(t) at infinity and the corresponding germ H^​(t)\hat{H}(t) do not depend on the choice of Γa,b.\Gamma_{a,b}.

After the change of variable z→P⁡(z)z\rightarrow P(z) integral (10) transforms to the Cauchy type integral

(11) H⁡(t)=∫γg⁡(z)​d​zz−t,H(t)=\int_{\gamma}\frac{g(z)dz}{z-t}\,,

where γ=P⁡(Γa,b)\gamma=P(\Gamma_{a,b}) and g⁡(z)g(z) is obtained by the analytic continuation along γ\gamma of a germ of the algebraic function Q​(P−1​(z)).Q(P^{-1}(z)). Clearly, integral representation (11) defines an analytic function in each domain of the complement of γ\gamma in ℂ​ℙ1{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}. Notice that for any choice of Γa,b\Gamma_{a,b} the function defined in the domain containing infinity is the analytic continuation of the germ H^​(t).\hat{H}(t).

Lemma 2.1 ([23]).

Assume that P⁡(z),P(z), q⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]q(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z] and a,b∈ℂ,a,b\in{\mathbb{C}}, a≠b,a\neq b, satisfy

(12) ∫Γa,bPi​(z)​q​(z)​𝑑z=0,i≥0,\int_{\Gamma_{a,b}}P^{i}(z)q(z){\rm d}z=0,\ \ \ i\geq 0,

and let Q⁡(z)Q(z) be a polynomial defined by the equalities

(13) Q⁡(z)=∫q⁡(z)​𝑑z,Q⁡(a)=0.Q(z)=\int q(z){\rm d}z,\ \ \ Q(a)=0.

Then for the germ H^​(t)\hat{H}(t) defined near infinity by integral (10) the equality H^​(t)≡0\hat{H}(t)\equiv 0 holds.

Proof. Indeed, for all i≥1i\geq 1 by integration by parts we have:

(14) ∫Γa,bPi​(z)​q​(z)​𝑑z=Pi​(b)​Q​(b)−Pi​(a)​Q​(a)−i​∫Γa,bPi−1​(z)​Q​(z)​P′​(z)​𝑑z.\int_{\Gamma_{a,b}}P^{i}(z)q(z){\rm d}z=P^{i}(b)Q(b)-P^{i}(a)Q(a)-i\int_{\Gamma_{a,b}}P^{i-1}(z)Q(z)P^{\prime}(z){\rm d}z.

Furthermore, Q⁡(a)=0Q(a)=0 implies Q⁡(b)=0Q(b)=0 in view of (12) taken for i=0i=0. Therefore, if (12) holds then all the integrals appearing in the right part of (14) vanish. On the other hand, these integrals are coefficients of the Taylor expansion of −H^​(t)-\hat{H}(t) at infinity. □\ \ \Box

Lemma 2.1 shows that the polynomial moment problem reduces to the problem of finding conditions on Q⁡(z)Q(z) under which the equality H^​(t)≡0\hat{H}(t)\equiv 0 holds. On the other hand, we will show below (Corollary 2.5) that if H^​(t)≡0\hat{H}(t)\equiv 0 holds for some polynomial Q⁡(z)Q(z) then (12) holds for q​(z)=Q′​(z).q(z)=Q^{\prime}(z). A condition of a general character for H^​(t)\hat{H}(t) to vanish was given in the paper [22] in the context of the theory of Cauchy type integrals of algebraic functions. Subsequently, in the paper [23] was proposed a construction which permits to obtain conditions for the vanishing of H^​(t)\hat{H}(t) in a very explicit form. Briefly, the idea of [23] is to choose the integration path Γa,b\Gamma_{a,b} in such a way that its image under the mapping P⁡(z):ℂ​ℙ1→ℂ​ℙ1P(z)\,:\,{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1} does not divide the Riemann sphere.

The construction of the paper [23] uses a special graph λP,\lambda_{P}, embedded into the Riemann sphere, defined as follows (see [23]). Let SS be a “star” joining a non-critical value cc of a polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) of degree nn with all its finite critical values c1,c2,…,ckc_{1},c_{2},...,c_{k} by non intersecting oriented arcs γ1,γ2,…,γk\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},...,\gamma_{k}. Define λP\lambda_{P} as a preimage of SS under the map P⁡(z):ℂ​ℙ1→ℂ​ℙ1P(z)\,:\,{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1} (see Fig. 1).

More precisely, define vertices of λP\lambda_{P} as preimages of the points cc and cs,c_{s}, 1≤s≤k,1\leq s\leq k, and edges of λP\lambda_{P} as preimages of the arcs γs,\gamma_{s}, 1≤s≤k.1\leq s\leq k. Furthermore, for each s,s, 1≤s≤k,1\leq s\leq k, mark vertices of λP\lambda_{P} which are preimages of the point csc_{s} by the number s.s. Finally, define a star of λP\lambda_{P} as a subset of edges of λP\lambda_{P} consisting of edges adjacent to some non-marked vertex.

By construction, the restriction of P⁡(z)P(z) on ℂ​ℙ1∖λP{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus\lambda_{P} is a covering of the topological punctured disk ℂ​ℙ1∖{S∪∞}{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus\{S\cup\infty\} and therefore ℂ​ℙ1∖λP{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus\lambda_{P} is a disjointed union of punctured disks (see e.g. [11]). Moreover, since the preimage of infinity under P⁡(z)P(z) consists of a unique point, ℂ​ℙ1∖λP{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus\lambda_{P} consists of a unique disk and hence the graph λP\lambda_{P} is a tree.

Set C={c1,c2,…,ck}C=\{c_{1},c_{2},...,c_{k}\} and let U⊂ℂU\subset{\mathbb{C}} be a simply connected domain such that S∖C⊂US\setminus C\subset U and U∩C=∅U\cap C=\emptyset. Then in UU there exist nn single-valued analytic branches of the algebraic function P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) inverse to P⁡(z).P(z). We will denote these branches by Pi−1​(z),P^{-1}_{i}(z), 1≤i≤n.1\leq i\leq n. The stars of λP\lambda_{P} may be naturally identified with branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in UU as follows: to the branch Pi−1​(z),P^{-1}_{i}(z), 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, corresponds the star Si,S_{i}, 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, such that Pi−1​(z)P^{-1}_{i}(z) maps bijectively the interior of SS to the interior of Si.S_{i}.

Under the analytic continuation along a closed curve the set Pi−1​(z),P^{-1}_{i}(z), 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, transforms to itself. This induces a homomorphism

(15) π1​(ℂ​ℙ1∖{C∪∞},c)→Sn\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus\{C\cup\infty\},c)\rightarrow S_{n}

whose image GPG_{P} is called the monodromy group of P⁡(z)P(z). Notice that if ω∞\omega_{\infty} and ωi\omega_{i}, 1≤i≤k,1\leq i\leq k, are loops around ∞\infty and cic_{i}, 1≤i≤k,1\leq i\leq k, respectively, such that ω1​ω2​…​ωk​ω∞=1\omega_{1}\omega_{2}\dots\omega_{k}\omega_{\infty}=1 in π1​(ℂ​ℙ1∖{C∪∞},c),\pi_{1}({\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus\{C\cup\infty\},c), then the elements gig_{i}, 1≤i≤k,1\leq i\leq k, of GPG_{P}, which are the images of ωi\omega_{i}, 1≤i≤k,1\leq i\leq k, under homomorphism (15), generate GPG_{P} and satisfy the equality g1​g2​…​gk​g∞=1,g_{1}g_{2}\dots g_{k}g_{\infty}=1, where g∞g_{\infty} is the element of GPG_{P} which is the image of ω∞\omega_{\infty}.

Having in mind the identification of the set of stars of λP\lambda_{P} with the set of branches of P−1​(z),P^{-1}(z), the permutation gs,g_{s}, 1≤s≤k,1\leq s\leq k, can be identified with a permutation g^s,\hat{g}_{s}, 1≤s≤k,1\leq s\leq k, acting on the set of stars of λP\lambda_{P} in the following way: g^s\hat{g}_{s} sends the star Si,S_{i}, 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, to the “next” star under a counterclockwise rotation around the vertex of SiS_{i} colored by the ssth color. For example, for the tree shown on Fig. 1 we have: g1=(1)​(2)​(37)​(4)​(5)​(6)​(8),g_{1}=(1)(2)(37)(4)(5)(6)(8), g2=(1)​(2)​(3)​(47)​(56)​(8),g_{2}=(1)(2)(3)(47)(56)(8), g3=(1238)​(4)​(57)​(6).g_{3}=(1238)(4)(57)(6). Notice that since P⁡(z)P(z) is a polynomial, the permutation g∞g_{\infty} is a cycle of length n.n. We always will assume that the numeration of branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in UU is chosen in such a way that g∞g_{\infty} coincides with the cycle (1 2​…​n)(1\,2\,...\,n). Clearly, such a numeration is defined uniquely up to a choice of P1−1​(z)P_{1}^{-1}(z).

The tree constructed above is known under the name of “constellation” or “cactus” and is closely related to what is called a “dessin d’enfant” (see [15] for further details and other versions of this construction). Notice that the Riemann existence theorem implies that a polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) is defined by c1,c2,…,ckc_{1},c_{2},...,c_{k} and λP\lambda_{P} up to a composition P⁡(z)→P⁡(μ⁡(z)),P(z)\rightarrow P(\mu(z)), where μ⁡(z)\mu(z) is a linear function.

It follows from the definition that the points aa and bb are vertices of λP\lambda_{P} if and only if P⁡(a)P(a) and P⁡(b)P(b) are critical values of P⁡(z)P(z). For our purposes however it is more convenient to define the tree λP\lambda_{P} so that the points a,ba,b always would be its vertices. So, in the case when P⁡(a)P(a) or P⁡(b)P(b) (or both of them) is not a critical value of P⁡(z)P(z) we modify the construction as follows. Define c1,c2,…,ckc_{1},c_{2},...,c_{k} as the set of all finite critical values of P⁡(z)P(z) supplemented by P⁡(a)P(a) or P⁡(b)P(b) (or by both of them), and set as above λP=P−1​{S},\lambda_{P}=P^{-1}\{S\}, where SS is a star connecting cc with c1,c2,…,ckc_{1},c_{2},...,c_{k} (we suppose that cc is chosen distinct from P⁡(a),P⁡(b)P(a),P(b)). Clearly, λP\lambda_{P} is still a tree and the points a,ba,b are vertices of λP.\lambda_{P}.

Since λP\lambda_{P} is connected and has no cycles there exists a unique oriented path μa,b⊂λP\mu_{a,b}\subset\lambda_{P} joining the point aa with the point bb. Furthermore, it follows from the definition of λP\lambda_{P} that if we set Γa,b=μa,b\Gamma_{a,b}=\mu_{a,b} then after the change of variable z→P⁡(z)z\rightarrow P(z) integral (10) reduces to the sum of integrals

(16) H⁡(t)=∑s=1k∫γsφs​(z)z−t​𝑑z,H(t)=\sum_{s=1}^{k}\int_{\gamma_{s}}\frac{{\varphi}_{s}(z)}{z-t}\,{\rm d}z,

where each φs​(z),{\varphi}_{s}(z), 1≤s≤k,1\leq s\leq k, is a linear combination of the functions Q​(Pi−1​(z)),Q(P^{-1}_{i}(z)), 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, in UU. Namely,

(17) φs​(z)=∑i=1nfs,i​Q​(Pi−1​(z)),{\varphi}_{s}(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{s,i}Q(P^{-1}_{i}(z)),

where fs,i≠0f_{s,i}\neq 0 if and only if the path μa,b\mu_{a,b} goes through the star SiS_{i} across its ss-vertex. Furthermore, if when going along μa,b\mu_{a,b} the ss-vertex of SiS_{i} is followed by the center of SiS_{i} then fs,i=−1f_{s,i}=-1 otherwise fs,i=1f_{s,i}=1. Theorem 2.2 ([23]).

The proposition below describes the position of branches appearing in Proposition 2.4 with respect to this numeration. More precisely, we describe the mutual position on the unit circle of the sets

V⁡(a)={εna1,εna2,…,εnada}andV⁡(b)={εnb1,εnb2,…,εnbdb},V(a)=\{{\varepsilon}_{n}^{a_{1}},{\varepsilon}_{n}^{a_{2}},...,{\varepsilon}^{a_{d_{a}}}_{n}\}\ \ \ \ \ {\rm and}\ \ \ \ \ V(b)=\{{\varepsilon}_{n}^{b_{1}},{\varepsilon}_{n}^{b_{2}},...,{\varepsilon}_{n}^{b_{d_{b}}}\},

where εn=e​x​p​(2​π​−1/n)\varepsilon_{n}=exp(2\pi\sqrt{-1}/n).

Let us introduce the following definitions. Say that two sets of points X,YX,Y on the unit circle S1S^{1} are disjointed if there exist s1,s2∈S1s_{1},s_{2}\in S^{1} such that one of two connected components of S1∖{s1,s2}S^{1}\setminus\{s_{1},s_{2}\} contains all points from XX while the other connected component of S1∖{s1,s2}S^{1}\setminus\{s_{1},s_{2}\} contains all points from Y.Y. Say that X,YX,Y are almost disjointed if X∩YX\cap Y consists of a single point s1s_{1} and there exists a point s2∈S1s_{2}\in S^{1} such that one of two connected components of S1∖{s1,s2}S^{1}\setminus\{s_{1},s_{2}\} contains all points from X∖s1X\setminus s_{1} while the other connected component of S1∖{s1,s2}S^{1}\setminus\{s_{1},s_{2}\} contains all points from Y∖s1.Y\setminus s_{1}.

Proposition 2.6 ([23]).

The sets V⁡(a)V(a) and V⁡(b)V(b) are disjointed or almost disjointed. Furthermore, if P⁡(a)=P⁡(b)P(a)=P(b) then V⁡(a)V(a) and V⁡(b)V(b) are disjointed.

Proof. Consider first the case when P⁡(a)=P⁡(b)=c1.P(a)=P(b)=c_{1}. Let U^\hat{U} be a simply-connected domain, containing no critical values of P⁡(z)P(z), such that U⊂U^U\subset\hat{U} and ∞∈∂U^\infty\in\partial\hat{U}. Any branch of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in UU can be extended analytically to U^\hat{U} and we will assume that the numeration of branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in U^\hat{U} is induced by the numeration of branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in U.U. Furthermore, let M⊂U^M\subset\hat{U} be a simple curve connecting points c1c_{1} and ∞\infty and Ω=P−1​{M}\Omega=P^{-1}\{M\} be the preimage of MM under the map P⁡(z):ℂ​ℙ1→ℂ​ℙ1.P(z)\,:\,{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\rightarrow{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}. It is convenient to consider Ω\Omega as a bicolored graph embedded into the Riemann sphere. Namely, we define black vertices of Ω\Omega as preimages of c1,c_{1}, a unique white vertex of Ω\Omega as the preimage of ∞,\infty, and edges of Ω\Omega as preimages of MM (see Fig. 3).

The edges of Ω\Omega may be identified with branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in U^\hat{U} as follows: to the branch Pi−1​(z),P^{-1}_{i}(z), 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, corresponds the edge eie_{i} such that Pi−1​(z)P^{-1}_{i}(z) maps bijectively the interior of MM to the interior of ei.e_{i}. In particular, the ordering of branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in U^\hat{U} induces the ordering of edges of Ω.\Omega. Since the multiplicity of the vertex ∞\infty equals nn and Ω\Omega has nn edges, Ω\Omega is connected.

Let EaE_{a} (resp. EbE_{b}) be a union of edges of Ω\Omega which are adjacent to the vertex aa (resp. bb). It follows from the bijectivity of branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) on the interior of MM that if DD is a domain from the collection of domains ℂ​ℙ1∖Ea{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus E_{a} such that b∈Db\in D, then DD contains the whole set Eb∖∞.E_{b}\setminus\infty. Now the proposition follows from the observation that the cyclic ordering of edges of Ω\Omega, induced by the cyclic ordering of branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in U^\hat{U}, coincides with the cyclic ordering of edges of Ω\Omega, induced by the orientation of ℂ​ℙ1{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1} in a neighborhood of infinity.

In the case when P⁡(a)≠P⁡(b)P(a)\neq P(b) the proof is modified as follows. Take two simple curves M1,M_{1}, M2⊂U^M_{2}\subset\hat{U} connecting the point ∞\infty with the points P⁡(a)P(a) and P⁡(b)P(b) correspondingly and consider the preimage P−1​{M1∪M2}P^{-1}\{M_{1}\cup M_{2}\} as a graph Ω\Omega embedded into the Riemann sphere. The vertices of Ω\Omega fall into three sets: the first one consists of a unique vertex which is the preimage of ∞,\infty, the second one consists of vertices which are preimages of P⁡(a),P(a), and the third one consists of vertices which are preimages of P⁡(b).P(b). Similarly, the edges of Ω\Omega fall into two sets: the first one consists of edges which are preimages of M1M_{1} and the second one consists of edges which are preimages of M2M_{2} (see Fig. 4).

Each of two sets of edges of Ω\Omega may be identified with branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in U^\hat{U} as follows: to the branch Pi−1​(z),P^{-1}_{i}(z), 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, corresponds the edge ei1e^{1}_{i} from the first set (resp. the edge ei2e^{2}_{i} from the second set) such that Pi−1​(z)P^{-1}_{i}(z) maps bijectively the interior of M1M_{1} (resp. of M2M_{2}) to the interior of ei1e^{1}_{i} (resp. of ei2e^{2}_{i}). The ordering of branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) in U^\hat{U} induces the ordering of edges of Ω\Omega in each of two sets. Clearly, this ordering coincides with the natural ordering induced by the orientation of ℂ​ℙ1.{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}. Furthermore, it is easy to see that when going round infinity in the counterclockwise direction the edge ei1,e^{1}_{i}, 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, is followed by the edge ei2.e^{2}_{i}.

Let Ea1E_{a}^{1} (resp. Eb2E_{b}^{2}) be a union of edges from the first (resp. the second) set Ω\Omega which are adjacent to the vertex aa (resp. bb). The bijectivity of branches of P−1​(z)P^{-1}(z) on the interior of M1M_{1} and M2M_{2} implies that if DD is a domain from the collection of domains ℂ​ℙ1∖Ea1{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus E_{a}^{1} such that b∈Db\in D, then DD contains the whole set Eb2∖∞.E_{b}^{2}\setminus\infty. Taking into account that for any k,k, 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, the edge ei1e^{1}_{i} is followed by ei2,e^{2}_{i}, this implies that V⁡(a)V(a) and V⁡(b)V(b) are disjointed or almost disjointed. □\ \ \Box

Remark. Since Q​(Pi−1​(z))Q(P^{-1}_{i}(z)), 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, are branches of an algebraic function, relations (19) are examples of linear relations between roots of an algebraic equation over the field ℂ⁡(z).{\mathbb{C}}(z). A general algebraic approach to such relations, over an arbitrary field, was developed in the papers [12], [13]. In particular, it follows from Theorem 1 of [13] that a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of at least one solution Q⁡(z)Q(z) of (19), such that the functions Q​(Pi−1​(z))Q(P^{-1}_{i}(z)), 1≤i≤n,1\leq i\leq n, are distinct between themselves, is that the subspace MP,a,bM_{P,a,b} does not contain elements of form (20). An equivalent form of this condition is that the subspace MP,a,bM_{P,a,b} does not contain any of subspaces Vd⟂,V_{d}^{\perp}, d∈D⁡(GP),d\in D(G_{P}), which are defined below. Notice however that the method of [13] does not provide any information about the description or the actual finding of these solutions.

3. Permutation matrix representations of groups containing a full cycle

3.1. Invariant subspaces and the centralizer ring

The construction of MP,a,bM_{P,a,b} implies that MP,a,bM_{P,a,b} is an invariant subspace of ℚn{\mathbb{Q}}^{n} with respect to the so called permutation matrix representation of the group GPG_{P} on ℚn.{\mathbb{Q}}^{n}. By definition, the permutation matrix representation of a transitive permutation group H⊆SnH\subseteq S_{n} on ℚn{\mathbb{Q}}^{n} is a homomorphism RH:H→G​Ln​(ℚ)R_{H}:\,H\rightarrow GL_{n}({\mathbb{Q}}) which associates to h∈Hh\in H a permutation matrix RH​(h)∈G​Ln​(ℚ)R_{H}(h)\in GL_{n}({\mathbb{Q}}) the elements ri,j,r_{i,j}, 1≤i,j≤n,1\leq i,j\leq n, of which satisfy ri,j=1r_{i,j}=1 if i=jhi=j^{h} and ri,j=0r_{i,j}=0 otherwise. In other words,

(x1x2xn)=RH​(h)​(x1hx2hxnh).\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}\\ x_{2}\\ \vdots\\ x_{n}\end{pmatrix}=R_{H}(h)\begin{pmatrix}x_{1^{h}}\\ x_{2^{h}}\\ \vdots\\ x_{n^{h}}\end{pmatrix}.

Note that ℚn{\mathbb{Q}}^{n} admits a RHR_{H}-invariant scalar product (x,y):=∑i=1nxi​yi(x,y):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}.

The goal of this section is to provide a full description of the invariant subspaces of ℚn{\mathbb{Q}}^{n} with respect to the permutation matrix representation of GPG_{P}. More general, we classify all invariant subspaces of ℚn{\mathbb{Q}}^{n} with respect to the permutation matrix representation of an arbitrary group G⊆SnG\subseteq S_{n} containing the cycle (1 2​…​n)(1\,2\,...\,n). In the following GG will always denote such a group.

Recall that a subset BB of X={1,2,…,n}X=\{1,2,\dots,n\} is called a block of a transitive permutation group H⊆SnH\subseteq S_{n} if for each h∈Hh\in H the set BhB^{h} is either disjoint or is equal to BB (see e.g. [28]). For a block BB the set ℬ:={Bh|h∈H}{\mathcal{B}}:=\{B^{h}\,|\,h\in H\} forms a partition of XX into a disjoint union of blocks of equal cardinality which is called an imprimitivity system of HH. Each permutation group H⊆SnH\subseteq S_{n} has two trivial imprimitivity systems: one formed by singletons and another formed by the whole XX. A permutation group is called primitive if it has only trivial imprimitivity systems. Otherwise it is called imprimitive.

For each d|nd\,|\,n we denote by VdV_{d} the subspace of ℚn{\mathbb{Q}}^{n} consisting of dd-periodic vectors. The fact that the group GG contains the cycle (1,…,n)(1,...,n) implies easily the following statement.

Lemma 3.1.

Any imprimitivity system for GG coincides with the residue classes modulo dd for some d|nd\,|\,n. Furthermore, for given dd such classes form an imprimitivity system for GG if and only if the subspace VdV_{d} is GG-invariant.□\ \ \Box

Denote by D⁡(G)D(G) the set of all divisors of nn for which VdV_{d} is GG-invariant. Clearly, 1,n∈D⁡(G)1,n\in D(G). Notice that D⁡(G)D(G) is a lattice with respect to the operations ∧,∨,\land,\lor, where d∧f:=gcd⁡(d,f)d\land f:=\gcd(d,f) and d∨f:=lcm⁡(d,f)d\lor f:={\rm lcm}(d,f). Indeed, for an element x∈Xx\in X the intersection of two blocks containing xx and corresponding to d,f∈D⁡(G)d,f\in D(G) is a block which corresponds to d∨fd\lor f. On the other hand, the intersection of two invariant subspaces Vd,VfV_{d},V_{f} is an invariant subspace which is equal to Vd∧f.V_{d\land f}.

We say that d∈D⁡(G)d\in D(G) covers f∈D⁡(G)f\in D(G) if f|d,f\,|\,d, f<d,f<d, and there is no x∈D⁡(G)x\in D(G) such that f<x<df<x<d and f|x,f|x, x|dx|d. Now we are ready to formulate the main result of this section.

Theorem 3.1.

Each RGR_{G}-irreducible subspace of ℚn{\mathbb{Q}}^{n} has the form

Ud:=Vd∩(Vf1⟂∩…∩Vfℓ⟂),U_{d}:=V_{d}\cap\left(V_{f_{1}}^{\perp}\cap...\cap V_{f_{\ell}}^{\perp}\right),

where d∈D⁡(G)d\in D(G) and f1,…,fℓf_{1},...,f_{\ell} is a complete set of elements of D⁡(G)D(G) covered by dd. The subspaces UdU_{d} are mutually orthogonal and every RGR_{G}-invariant subspace of ℚn{\mathbb{Q}}^{n} is a direct sum of some UdU_{d} as above.

The proof of this theorem splits into several steps and is given below. We start from recalling some basic facts of the representations theory which we will use afterward (see e.g. [14]).

First, any representation TH:H→G​Ln​(k)T_{H}:\,H\rightarrow GL_{n}(k) of a finite group HH over a field kk of characteristic not dividing |H||H| is completely reducible, that is knk^{n} is a direct sum of THT_{H}-invariant irreducible subspaces (Maschke’s theorem). Furthermore, irreducible subspaces of a completely reducible representation TH:H→G​Ln​(k)T_{H}:\,H\rightarrow GL_{n}(k) are in one-to-one correspondence with minimal idempotents of the centralizer ring Vk​(TH)V_{k}(T_{H}). Recall that Vk​(TH)V_{k}(T_{H}) consists of all matrices A∈Mn​(k)A\in M_{n}(k) which commute with every TH​(h),h∈H.T_{H}(h),h\in H. Furthermore, a matrix EE is called an idempotent if E≠0E\neq 0 and E2=EE^{2}=E. Two idempotents E,FE,F are called orthogonal if E​F=F​E=0EF=FE=0. Finally, an idempotent E∈Vk​(TH)E\in V_{k}(T_{H}) is called minimal if it can not be presented as a sum of two orthogonal idempotents from Vk​(TH)V_{k}(T_{H}). Under this notation the correspondence above is obtained as follows: to a minimal idempotent E∈Vk​(TH)E\in V_{k}(T_{H}) corresponds an irreducible subspace V=𝖨𝗆​{E}.V={\sf Im}\{E\}.

In general, the decomposition of knk^{n} into a sum of THT_{H}-invariant irreducible subspaces is not uniquely defined. Nevertheless, if

(26) kn=V1⊕a1⊕⋯⊕Vr⊕ark^{n}=V_{1}^{\oplus a_{1}}\oplus\dots\oplus V_{r}^{\oplus a_{r}}

is a decomposition such that Vi,V_{i}, 1≤i≤r,1\leq i\leq r, are pairwise non-isomorphic THT_{H}-invariant irreducible subspaces of knk^{n}, then the subspaces Vi⊕ai,V_{i}^{\oplus a_{i}}, 1≤i≤r,1\leq i\leq r, are defined uniquely. They correspond to the minimal idempotents of the center C​(Vk​(TH))C(V_{k}(T_{H})) of the centralizer ring Vk​(TH).V_{k}(T_{H}). Furthermore, Vk​(TH)V_{k}(T_{H}) is commutative if and only if ai=1a_{i}=1 for all i,i, 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r. Notice that if Vk​(TH)V_{k}(T_{H}) is commutative and the space knk^{n} admits a THT_{H}-invariant scalar product then all THT_{H}-invariant irreducible subspaces of knk^{n} are mutually orthogonal. Indeed, for any representation TH:H→G​Ln​(k)T_{H}:\,H\rightarrow GL_{n}(k), which admits an invariant scalar product, knk^{n} can be decomposed into a sum of THT_{H}-invariant irreducible subspaces

(27) kn=V1⊕⋯⊕Vrk^{n}=V_{1}\oplus\dots\oplus V_{r}

with mutually orthogonal ViV_{i}. On the other hand, if Vk​(TH)V_{k}(T_{H}) is commutative then a decomposition of THT_{H} into a sum of THT_{H}-invariant irreducible subspaces is uniquely defined and therefore coincides with (27).

For the permutation matrix representation RH:H→G​Ln​(k)R_{H}:\,H\rightarrow GL_{n}(k) of a transitive permutation group H⊆SnH\subseteq S_{n} instead of the notation Vk​(RH)V_{k}(R_{H}) we will use simply the symbol Vk​(H).V_{k}(H). Below we will show (Proposition 3.5) that for any group GG as above the ring Vℚ​(G)V_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G) is isomorphic to a subring of the group algebra of a cyclic group and hence is commutative. Therefore, the above remarks imply the following statement.

Proposition 3.2.

An RGR_{G}-invariant subspace W⊂ℚnW\subset{{\mathbb{Q}}}^{n} is irreducible if and only if there exists a minimal idempotent E∈Vℚ​(G)E\in V_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G) such that 𝖨𝗆​{E}=W{\sf Im}\{E\}=W. RGR_{G}-invariant irreducible subspaces of ℚn{\mathbb{Q}}^{n} are mutually orthogonal and every RGR_{G}-invariant subspace is a direct sum of some WW as above. □\ \ \Box

For each transitive permutation group H⊆SnH\subseteq S_{n} we can construct some special basis of Vℂ​(H)V_{\mathbb{C}}(H) via orbits of the stabilizer H1H_{1} of the point 1 as follows. 3.2. Schur rings

3.2.1. Isomorphism between Sℚ​(G)S_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G) and Vℚ​(G)V_{\mathbb{Q}}(G)

In order to construct the minimal idempotents of Vℚ​(G)V_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G) we will use so called Schur rings introduced by Schur in his classical paper [27] for the investigation of permutation groups containing a regular subgroup CC. Since in this paper CC always will be a cyclic group, in the following we will restrict our attention to this case only (see [28] for the account of the Schur method in the general case).

The idea of the Schur approach can be described as follows. If G⊆SnG\subseteq S_{n} contains the cycle c:=(1 2​…​n)c:=(1\,2\,...\,n) then elements of the set {1,2,…,n}\left\{1,2,\dots,n\right\} can be identified with elements of the cyclic group CC generated by cc as follows: to the element ii corresponds the element of CC which transforms 11 to ii. Therefore, we can consider GG as a permutation group acting on its subgroup C.C. After such an identification we can “multiply” elements of the set {1,2,…,n}\left\{1,2,\dots,n\right\} and this multiplication agrees with the action of GG in the following sense: if h,g∈Ch,g\in C then hg=h​gh^{g}=hg. Furthermore, identifying any two subsets of {1,2,…,n}\left\{1,2,\dots,n\right\} with the corresponding elements of the group algebra ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C] we can define their “product” as the product of these elements in ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C]. The remarkable result of Schur is that under such a multiplication the orbits of the stabilizer G1G_{1} form a basis of some subalgebra of ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C]. To make this statement precise let us introduce the following definition.

For T⊆CT\subseteq C denote by T(−1)T^{\left(-1\right)} the set of elements of CC inverse to the elements of TT and by T¯\underline{T} the formal sum ∑h∈Th\sum_{h\in T}h. The elements of ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C] of the form T¯\underline{T} for some T⊆CT\subseteq C are called simple quantities ([28]).

Definition 3.4.

A subalgebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} of the group algebra ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C] is called a Schur ring or an S-ring over CC if it satisfies the following axioms:

  • (S1)

    𝒜\mathcal{A} as a ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-module has a basis consisting of simple quantities T0¯,…,Td¯\underline{T_{0}},\dots,\underline{T_{d}}, where T0={e}T_{0}=\{e\},

  • (S2)

    Ti∩Tj=∅T_{i}\cap T_{j}=\emptyset for i≠ji\neq j and ⋃j=0dTj=C\bigcup_{j=0}^{d}T_{j}=C,

  • (S3)

    For each i∈{0,1,…,d}i\in\{0,1,\dots,d\} there exists i′∈{0,1,…,d}i^{\prime}\in\{0,1,\dots,d\} such that Ti′=Ti(−1)T_{i^{\prime}}=T_{i}{}^{(-1)}.

It is easy to see that the basis T0¯,…,Td¯\underline{T_{0}},\dots,\underline{T_{d}} satisfying (S1) and (S2) is unique. Such a basis is called the standard basis of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The number d+1d+1 is called the rank of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The sets TiT_{i}, 0≤i≤d0\leq i\leq d, are called the basic sets of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Finally, the notation 𝒜=⟨T0¯,…,Td¯⟩\mathcal{A}=\langle\underline{T_{0}},\dots,\underline{T_{d}}\rangle is used if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is an S-ring over CC whose basic sets are T0,…,TdT_{0},\dots,T_{d}. We also write 𝖡𝖺𝗌𝗂𝖼⁡(𝒜){\sf Basic}(\mathcal{A}) for the set {T0,…,Td}\{T_{0},\dots,T_{d}\}. Notice that if 𝒜~\tilde{\mathcal{A}} is an SS-ring which is a subring of 𝒜\mathcal{A} then its basic sets are some unions of basic sets of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. There are two trivial S-rings, namely ⟨e¯,C∖{e}¯⟩\langle\underline{e},\underline{C\setminus\{e\}}\rangle and ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C].

Proposition 3.5.

To any group GG corresponds a Schur ring Sℚ​(G)S_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G) the basic sets of which are the orbits of the stabilizer G1G_{1}. Moreover, Sℚ​(G)S_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G) and Vℚ​(G)V_{\mathbb{Q}}(G) are isomorphic as ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}-algebras.

The Proposition 3.5 is a particular case of Theorem 28.8 in [28]. It implies in particular that in order to describe the minimal idempotents of Vℚ​(G)V_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G) it is enough to describe the ones of Sℚ​(G)S_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G). Since however for this purpose an explicit construction of the isomorphism between Sℚ​(G)S_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G) and Vℚ​(G)V_{\mathbb{Q}}(G) is needed, we give below a short proof of Proposition 3.5 which is based on Proposition 3.3

Proof of Proposition 3.5. First of all observe that since GG contains cc each matrix M∈Vℚ​(G)M\in V_{\mathbb{Q}}(G) is necessarily a circulant that is each row vector of MM is cyclically shifted for one element to the right relative to the preceding row vector, in other words

(28) Mi,j=M1,j−i+1​mod​n.M_{i,j}=M_{1,j-i+1\,{\rm mod\ }n}.

Define now a mapping ψ:Vℚ​(G)→ℚ⁡[C]\psi:V_{\mathbb{Q}}(G)\rightarrow{\mathbb{Q}}[C] by the formula

ψ⁡(M):=∑j=1nM1,j​cj−1\psi(M):=\sum_{j=1}^{n}M_{1,j}c^{j-1}

and show that ψ\psi is an algebra monomorphism. Indeed, for any M,N∈Vℚ​(G)M,N\in V_{\mathbb{Q}}(G) we have:

ψ⁡(M​N)=∑ℓ=1n(M​N)1,ℓ​cℓ−1=∑ℓ=1n∑i=1nM1,i​Ni,ℓ​cℓ−1=\psi(MN)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}(MN)_{1,\ell}c^{\ell-1}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}M_{1,i}N_{i,\ell}c^{\ell-1}=
=∑ℓ=1n∑i=1nM1,i​N1,ℓ−i+1​cℓ−1=∑i=1n∑j=1nM1,i​N1,j​ci+j−2==\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}M_{1,i}N_{1,\ell-i+1}c^{\ell-1}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}M_{1,i}N_{1,j}c^{i+j-2}=
=(∑i=1nM1,i​ci−1)​(∑j=1nN1,j​cj−1)=ψ⁡(M)​ψ​(N).=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}M_{1,i}c^{i-1}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}N_{1,j}c^{j-1}\right)=\psi(M)\psi(N).

Thus ψ\psi is an algebra homomorphism. Furthermore, ψ\psi is injective since any matrix M∈Vℚ​(G)M\in V_{\mathbb{Q}}(G) is defined by its first row in view of (28).

Clearly, the image of Vℚ​(G)V_{\mathbb{Q}}(G) is a subalgebra Sℚ​(G)S_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G) of ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C]. Furthermore, by construction, the basis of this subalgebra consists of the orbits of the stabilizer G1.G_{1}. The properties S1, S2 of Sℚ​(G)S_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G) are obvious. Finally, since any matrix from Vℚ​(G)V_{\mathbb{Q}}(G) is a circulant, it follows from the third part of Proposition 3.3 that Δ(−1)=Γ\Delta^{(-1)}=\Gamma. □\ \ \Box

For dd dividing nn denote by CdC_{d} a unique subgroup of CC of order dd. For a Schur ring 𝒜\mathcal{A} denote by D⁡(𝒜)D(\mathcal{A}) a set consisting of all divisors of nn for which Cd¯∈𝒜\underline{C_{d}}\in\mathcal{A}.

Lemma 3.6.

d∈D⁡(G)⇔n/d∈D⁡(Sℚ​(G))d\in D(G)\iff n/d\in D(S_{{\mathbb{Q}}}(G)).

Proof. Let d∈D⁡(G)d\in D(G). Then Cn/dC_{n/d} under the identification of the set {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\dots,n\} with CC corresponds to the set X={1,d+1,2​d+1,…,n−d+1}X=\{1,d+1,2d+1,\dots,n-d+1\} and therefore is a block of GG containing 1. 3.2.2. Rational SS-rings

The automorphism group of CC is isomorphic to the multiplicative group ℤn∗{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*}. Namely, to the element m∈ℤn∗m\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*} corresponds the automorphism g↦gm,g∈C.g\mapsto g^{m},g\in C. Extending this action onto ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C] by linearity we obtain an action of ℤn∗{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*} on the group algebra ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C]:

α=∑g∈Cαg​g⟶α(m):=∑g∈Cαg​gm.\alpha=\sum_{g\in C}\alpha_{g}g\ \ \longrightarrow\ \alpha^{(m)}:=\sum_{g\in C}\alpha_{g}g^{m}.

An element α∈ℚ⁡[C]\alpha\in{\mathbb{Q}}[C] is called rational if α=α(m)\alpha=\alpha^{(m)} for any m∈ℤn∗m\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*}. Note that the mappings α↦α(m),\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{(m)}, m∈ℤn∗m\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*}, are automorphisms of ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C]. Moreover, these mappings are automorphisms of any S-ring 𝒜\mathcal{A} over CC (see [28], Theorem 23.9). In particular, for each m∈ℤn∗m\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*} and T⊆CT\subseteq C we have

T∈𝖡𝖺𝗌𝗂𝖼⁡(𝒜)⇔T(m)∈𝖡𝖺𝗌𝗂𝖼⁡(𝒜),T\in{\sf Basic}(\mathcal{A})\iff T^{(m)}\in{\sf Basic}(\mathcal{A}),

where for a subset T⊂CT\subset C by T(m)T^{(m)} is denoted the set of mm-th powers of elements of TT.

Recall that the set of all irreducible complex representations of CC consists of nn one-dimensional representations (characters) χ0,…,χn−1\chi_{0},...,\chi_{n-1} where

χℓ​(cj):=e2​π​−1​ℓ​j/n, 0≤j,ℓ≤n−1.\chi_{\ell}(c^{j}):=e^{2\pi\sqrt{-1}\ell j/n},\ \ 0\leq j,\ell\leq n-1.

We will keep the same notation for the extensions of χ0,…,χn−1\chi_{0},...,\chi_{n-1} by linearity on ℚ⁡[C]{\mathbb{Q}}[C]. The rational elements of an SS-ring 𝒜\mathcal{A} admit the following characterization.

Lemma 3.7.

An element α∈ℚ⁡[C]\alpha\in{\mathbb{Q}}[C] is rational if and only if χl​(α)∈ℚ\chi_{l}(\alpha)\in{\mathbb{Q}} for all l,l, 0≤l≤n−1.0\leq l\leq n-1.

Proof. The group Γ\Gamma is isomorphic to ℤn∗{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*}. Namely, to the element m∈ℤn∗m\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*} corresponds the element σm∈Γ\sigma_{m}\in\Gamma which transforms e2​π​−1/ne^{2\pi\sqrt{-1}/n} to e2​π​−1​m/ne^{2\pi\sqrt{-1}m/n}. We have:

An SS-ring 𝒜\mathcal{A} is called rational if all its elements are rational. Clearly, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is rational if and only if T(m)=TT^{(m)}=T for all T∈𝖡𝖺𝗌𝗂𝖼⁡(𝒜)T\in{\sf Basic}(\mathcal{A}) and m∈ℤn∗m\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*}. Any rational SS-ring is a subring of some universal rational SS-ring W.W. To construct WW observe that the orbits of the action of ℤn∗{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*} on CC are parametrized by the divisors of nn as follows: an orbit Om,O_{m}, m|n,m|n, consists of all generators of the group CmC_{m}. It turns out that the vector space spanned by Om¯,\underline{O_{m}}, m|nm|n, is a rational SS-ring WW ([27]). Furthermore, any rational SS-ring 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a subring of W.W. Indeed, since any element of the standard basis of a rational SS-ring 𝒜\mathcal{A} is invariant with respect to the action of ℤn∗,{\mathbb{Z}}_{n}^{*}, such an element is a union of some Om,O_{m}, m|n.m|n. Therefore, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a subring of W.W.

Remark. Theorem 1.1 implies that if for a given polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) the corresponding polynomial moment problem has non-reducible solutions, then P⁡(z)P(z) has at least one “double decomposition”

P=A∘B=C∘DP=A\circ B=C\circ D

B⁡(z)∉ℂ⁡(D⁡(z)),D⁡(z)∉ℂ⁡(B⁡(z)).B(z)\notin{\mathbb{C}}(D(z)),\ \ \ D(z)\notin{\mathbb{C}}(B(z)).

Notice that this condition is quite restrictive. Namely, the results of Engstrom [10] and Ritt [24] imply that if polynomials A,B,A,B, C,DC,D satisfy the equation

and up to a possible replacement of A^\hat{A} by C^\hat{C} and B^\hat{B} by D^\hat{D} either

where Tn​(z),Tm​(z)T_{n}(z),T_{m}(z) are the corresponding Chebyshev polynomials, n,m≥1,n,m\geq 1, and GCD⁡(n,m)=1.{\rm GCD}(n,m)=1.
